subject: chemistry
title: Metals vs Non-metals
welcome_lead: Shiny, bendy, buzzing with current: meet the metallic family.
meta_desc: Compare metals and non-metals in this KS3 chemistry adventure on physical properties.
final_note: You can now classify any element as a metal or non-metal by its properties.

concepts.def: Shiny, conducts heat and electricity, malleable.
Dull, poor conductor, often brittle if solid.
Can be hammered into shape without breaking.
Allows heat or electricity to flow through it.
Does not let heat or electricity flow easily.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Most metals are shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (bendable) and ductile (can be drawn into wires).

Most are solid at room temperature, with high melting points. Mercury is the exception — it is a liquid metal!

Non-metals are usually dull, poor conductors (insulators), and often brittle if solid. Many are gases at room temperature.

Examples: oxygen, sulfur, carbon, chlorine.

Copper wires carry electricity — they are a great conductor. Plastic around the wire is a great insulator and keeps you safe.

Match the property to the job.

mcqs.q: How is a dynamic equilibrium different from a static one?
options: In a dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; in a static equilibrium, nothing is happening at the particle level.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
A dynamic equilibrium means the system is still changing visibly.
Dynamic and static equilibria are the same thing because both show constant macroscopic properties.

mcqs.q: In a standard hydrogen electrode used as a reference, what is the assigned electrode potential?
options: The standard hydrogen electrode actually has zero potential because hydrogen has no charge.
A dynamic equilibrium means the system is still changing visibly.
Exactly 0 V by convention — all other electrode potentials are measured relative to it.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the fingerprint region (below ~1500 cm^-1) in IR spectroscopy?
options: The fingerprint region is used to identify which functional groups are present.
The fingerprint region is the part that contains all the most useful absorptions.
A dynamic equilibrium means the system is still changing visibly.
It is unique to each compound — used to identify a specific molecule by matching to a known spectrum.
